cse-2025-2-cs-17.approach: Reconstruct the interleaving that produces exactly the reported balances, then test each ACID property against what that schedule provably did. Only properties whose violation is *forced* by the facts count ("certain to have been violated").
cse-2025-2-cs-17.given:
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Initial balance of $A$ | Rs. 11000 |
| Each transfer | Rs. 10000 from $A$ to $B$ |
| Both transactions read $A$ as | Rs. 11000 |
| $B$ credited | Rs. 10000 **twice** |
| Final balance of $A$ | Rs. 1000 (debited once) |

steps.title: Reconstruct the schedule
steps.body:
Both transactions read $A = 11000$ before either wrote, each computed $11000 - 10000 = 1000$ and wrote it. The second write simply overwrote the first with the same stale value — a classic **lost update**:

$R_1(A),\ R_2(A),\ W_1(A{=}1000),\ W_1(B{+}10000),\ W_2(A{=}1000),\ W_2(B{+}10000)$

steps.title: Isolation: violated
steps.body: In any serial order the second transaction would read $A = 1000$, not $11000$. Here both read $11000$, so the result ($A = 1000$, $B$ credited $20000$) matches **no** serial schedule. Concurrent execution leaked into the result, which is exactly what isolation forbids.

steps.title: Consistency: violated
steps.body:
Invariant of a transfer system: total money is conserved, $A + B$ unchanged.

Before: $A + B = 11000 + B_0$. After: $A + B = 1000 + (B_0 + 20000) = B_0 + 21000$.

The bank created $21000 - 11000 = 10000$ rupees. Also, $A$ could fund only one transfer ($11000 < 2 \times 10000$), so the second one should have been refused. The database moved from a consistent state to an **inconsistent** one.

steps.title: Atomicity and durability: not certainly violated
steps.body:
- **Atomicity** (all-or-nothing): each transaction performed *all* of its operations — it wrote $A$ and credited $B$. No transaction stopped half-way, so nothing proves an atomicity failure.
- **Durability** (committed effects survive failures): no crash or lost commit is reported; every write that was made is still there. The "missing" debit was never *computed* correctly — it was overwritten by a concurrent write, which is an isolation problem, not a durability one.

So the properties certain to be violated are **Consistency** and **Isolation**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Each transfer executed both its debit write and its credit — neither stopped half-way, so there is no evidence of a partial (non-atomic) transaction.
Money is not conserved: $A + B$ grew by Rs. 10000, and an overdraft that should have been refused went through — the final state breaks the integrity constraint.
Both transactions read the same pre-update value Rs. 11000; no serial order produces that, so the interleaving was visible — a lost update.
Durability concerns committed data surviving failures. No failure occurred and no committed write was undone by a crash; the overwrite came from concurrency control.

cse-2025-2-cs-17.shortcut: Two transactions "read the same initial value" of a shared item and one update vanished = lost update ⇒ Isolation. Money appeared from nowhere ⇒ Consistency.
pitfalls: Marking Durability because "one debit was lost" — it was overwritten by a concurrent write, not lost to a crash.
Marking Atomicity: atomicity is about a single transaction completing partially; here both ran to completion.
cse-2025-2-cs-17.verification: A serial run (T1 then T2) gives: T1 sets $A = 1000$, $B = B_0 + 10000$; T2 reads $1000$, cannot transfer 10000 (or would make $A = -9000$). Either way the observed $A = 1000$ with two credits never arises serially, confirming the isolation failure and the broken money invariant.

cse-2025-2-cs-18.approach: Separate the **architecture** (the contract a compiler/assembly programmer sees: instructions, registers, addressing modes, data types, memory model) from the **microarchitecture/implementation** (caches, clock speed, pipelines). Only the former is part of the ISA.

steps.title: What the ISA specifies
steps.body: The ISA is the hardware–software interface: the instruction formats and opcodes, the **programmer-visible registers** (how many, how wide), addressing modes, data types and the memory model. Two processors with the same ISA run the same binaries.

steps.title: Registers are architectural
steps.body: Register-operand instructions carry a register-number field (e.g. 5 bits for 32 registers in MIPS/RISC-V). The compiler allocates variables to these named registers, so the **total number of registers** is fixed by the ISA — change it and every binary changes.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body:
| Option | Visible to machine code? | Part of ISA? |
|---|---|---|
| Cache size | No — transparent to software | No |
| Clock frequency | No — same binary runs at any speed | No |
| Number of cache levels | No — implementation choice | No |
| Number of registers | Yes — register fields in instructions name them | **Yes** |

For example, Intel Core i3 and i9 share the x86-64 ISA (16 general-purpose registers) but differ in cache sizes, cache levels and clock rates.

answer.value: **The total number of registers** — option (D) only

optionAnalysis.reason: Caches are invisible to the instruction set; changing the cache size does not change a single instruction. It is a microarchitecture parameter.
Clock frequency is an implementation/performance property; the same ISA is sold at many frequencies.
L1/L2/L3 organisation is a microarchitecture decision, transparent to programs.
Registers are programmer-visible state; instructions encode register numbers, so their count is fixed by the ISA (e.g. 32 integer registers in MIPS/RISC-V).

cse-2025-2-cs-18.shortcut: Ask: "would a compiled program have to change if this changed?" Only the register count passes.
pitfalls: Thinking cache parameters are architectural because they affect performance — performance is not part of the ISA contract.
cse-2025-2-cs-18.verification: Same-ISA families (x86-64 laptops vs. servers, ARMv8 phones vs. Apple M-series) differ widely in cache size, levels and clock, yet run identical binaries — they agree only on the register set and instructions.

cse-2025-2-cs-19.approach: Use the two structural facts: in an **undirected** DFS every non-tree edge joins an ancestor and a descendant (no cross edges), and in BFS every edge joins vertices whose levels differ by at most 1. Then a tiny counterexample kills (A).

steps.title: (A) DFS tree need not be a shortest-path tree
steps.body: Triangle $s, a, b$ with edges $sa, ab, sb$. DFS from $s$ may go $s \to a \to b$, putting $b$ at depth $2$, but $d(s, b) = 1$ via edge $sb$. So a DFS tree is **not** a shortest-path tree in general. **False.**

scene.caption: DFS tree (blue) puts b at depth 2; the non-tree edge sb is a back edge.

steps.title: (B) Undirected DFS has only tree and back edges
steps.body: Suppose $(u, v)$ is a non-tree edge and $u$ is discovered first. While $u$ is still active, DFS explores all of $u$'s neighbours, including $v$ (still white), so $v$ is discovered **inside** $u$'s subtree. Hence $v$ is a descendant of $u$: the edge connects ancestor and descendant — a back edge (a forward edge seen from $u$). Cross edges cannot occur. **True.**

steps.title: (C) BFS: levels of an edge differ by at most 1
steps.body: BFS gives $d(x) = $ true distance from $s$. For any edge $(u, v)$: $d(v) \le d(u) + 1$ and $d(u) \le d(v) + 1$, so $\lvert d(u) - d(v) \rvert \le 1$. This holds for every edge, in particular every non-tree edge. **True.**

steps.title: (D) Both find connected components
steps.body: Run BFS (or DFS) from any unvisited vertex; it visits exactly that vertex's component. Repeat until all vertices are visited: each run = one component, $O(V + E)$ total. **True.**

optionAnalysis.reason: Counterexample: triangle s–a–b; DFS s→a→b gives b depth 2 while its distance is 1. BFS trees, not DFS trees, are shortest-path trees in unweighted graphs.
In an undirected DFS a non-tree edge always joins an ancestor and a descendant — back edge (forward from the other end); cross edges are impossible.
BFS levels equal true distances, and adjacent vertices' distances differ by at most 1.
One traversal from an unvisited vertex marks one whole component; repeating gives all components with either BFS or DFS.

cse-2025-2-cs-19.shortcut: Undirected DFS: tree + back edges only. Undirected BFS: tree + edges within the same level or adjacent levels.
pitfalls: Carrying over directed-graph DFS classification (cross edges exist only in directed graphs).
Assuming any spanning tree from a traversal gives shortest paths — only BFS does (unweighted).
cse-2025-2-cs-19.verification: On the triangle: BFS from s puts a and b both at level 1, and non-tree edge ab joins levels 1 and 1 (difference 0 ≤ 1), consistent with (C); the DFS run has only the back edge sb, consistent with (B).

animation.title: Counterexample for (A): DFS on a triangle

cse-2025-2-cs-20.approach: Write down, for each class, which of the three properties (a), (b), (c) hold. Several items can legitimately match each class, so an option is correct when **every** pair it states is a true fact.

steps.title: CFLs
steps.body: CFLs are closed under union ($S \to S_1 \mid S_2$) but **not** under intersection: $\{a^nb^nc^m\} \cap \{a^mb^nc^n\} = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not context-free. Since $L_1 \cap L_2 = \overline{\bar L_1 \cup \bar L_2}$ and union is closed, complement **cannot** be closed either. So (i) satisfies (a) and (b), not (c).

steps.title: Property table
steps.body:
| Class | (a) closed under ∪ | (b) NOT closed under complement | (c) closed under ∩ |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) CFL | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| (ii) Recursive | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |
| (iii) Regular | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |

CFLs: $L_1 \cup L_2$ via $S \to S_1 \mid S_2$; not closed under ∩ ($a^nb^nc^m \cap a^mb^nc^n = a^nb^nc^n$), hence not under complement (De Morgan). Recursive: a decider can run both deciders, or flip its answer. Regular: product DFA / swap final states.

steps.title: Check each option pair by pair
steps.body:
- (A): (ii)–(b) claims recursive languages are not closed under complement — false.
- (B): (i)–(b) ✓, (ii)–(a) ✓, (iii)–(c) ✓ — **correct**.
- (C): (i)–(b) ✓, (ii)–(c) ✓, (iii)–(a) ✓ — **correct**.
- (D): (iii)–(b) claims regular languages are not closed under complement — false.

optionAnalysis.reason: (i)–(a) and (iii)–(c) are true, but (ii)–(b) is false: recursive languages ARE closed under complementation (swap accept/reject of the decider).
CFLs are not closed under complement, recursive languages are closed under union, regular languages are closed under intersection — all true.
CFLs not closed under complement, recursive closed under intersection, regular closed under union — all true.
(iii)–(b) is false: regular languages are closed under complementation (complement the final states of a DFA).

cse-2025-2-cs-20.shortcut: Among the three classes only CFLs fail complementation, so (b) can pair only with (i). That kills (A) and (D) immediately; (B) and (C) contain only true facts.
pitfalls: Treating it as a one-to-one matching and rejecting (B) or (C) because each class can satisfy several properties.
Forgetting that CFLs are closed under union but not intersection.
cse-2025-2-cs-20.verification: Recheck (b): the only class not closed under complement is CFL; (A) pairs (b) with recursive and (D) with regular, both wrong; (B) and (C) both pair (b) with CFL.

cse-2025-2-cs-21.approach: Read the three OR inputs off the diagram, write $F$, and simplify with absorption. Then test each option for equality with the simplified function.
cse-2025-2-cs-21.given: OR gate inputs: NAND$(X, Y)$, NOT $X$, and AND$(X, \bar Y)$.

steps.title: Write F from the circuit
steps.body:
Top gate: NAND of $Y$ and $X$ → $\overline{XY}$. Middle: inverter on $X$ → $\bar X$. Bottom: AND of $X$ and $\bar Y$ → $X\bar Y$. The OR gives

$$F = \overline{XY} + \bar X + X\bar Y.$$

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body:
De Morgan: $\overline{XY} = \bar X + \bar Y$. So

$$F = \bar X + \bar Y + \bar X + X\bar Y = \bar X + \bar Y + X\bar Y.$$

Absorption ($\bar Y + X\bar Y = \bar Y(1 + X) = \bar Y$):

$$F = \bar X + \bar Y = \overline{XY}.$$

So $F$ is 0 only for $X = Y = 1$ (shown in the frame).

steps.title: Check with another input
steps.body: For $X = 1, Y = 0$: NAND $= 1$, so $F = 1$. Indeed $\overline{1 \cdot 0} = 1$. Any input with a 0 makes $F = 1$; only $11$ gives $0$ — exactly NAND.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body:
- (A) $\overline{XY}$ = simplified $F$ ✓
- (B) $\bar X + \bar Y + X\bar Y = \bar X + \bar Y$ ✓ (absorption)
- (C) is $F$ written exactly as read from the gates ✓
- (D) $X + \bar Y$: at $X = 1, Y = 1$ it is $1$ but $F = 0$ ✗

optionAnalysis.reason: After De Morgan and absorption, $F = \bar X + \bar Y = \overline{XY}$.
It equals $\overline{XY} + X\bar Y$ rewritten by De Morgan; the $X\bar Y$ term is absorbed by $\bar Y$, giving $\overline{XY}$.
This is literally the OR of the three gate outputs, i.e. $F$ before simplification.
At $X = 1, Y = 1$: $X + \bar Y = 1$ but $F = 0$. It would come from misreading the middle inverter as a buffer.

cse-2025-2-cs-21.shortcut: One OR input is already $\overline{XY}$, and the other two ($\bar X$, $X\bar Y$) imply it (each is 1 only when $XY = 0$), so they add nothing: $F = \overline{XY}$.
pitfalls: Missing the bubble on the top gate (AND vs NAND).
Not realising an MSQ can have several equivalent expressions all correct.
cse-2025-2-cs-21.verification: Truth table: $XY = 00, 01, 10, 11$ gives $F = 1, 1, 1, 0$ (NAND) and option (B)/(C) give $1, 1, 1, 0$ as well, while (D) gives $1, 0, 1, 1$.

cse-2025-2-cs-22.approach: Booth's algorithm (radix-2) scans the multiplier pairs $(Q_i, Q_{i-1})$ with $Q_{-1} = 0$: pair $10$ ⇒ subtract $M$, $01$ ⇒ add $M$, $00$/$11$ ⇒ shift only. So the count is just the number of bit **changes** in $Q$ with a $0$ appended on the right; $M$ is irrelevant.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body:
At each of the 16 iterations look at $(Q_i, Q_{i-1})$:

| pair | action |
|---|---|
| 00, 11 | shift only |
| 10 | $A \leftarrow A - M$, then shift |
| 01 | $A \leftarrow A + M$, then shift |

So every place where adjacent bits of $Q\,0$ differ costs one add/sub.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
Subtractions: $4 + 3 = 7$. Additions: $3 + 3 = 6$.

$$7 + 6 = 13$$

add/sub operations.

cse-2025-2-cs-22.shortcut: Write $Q$ followed by $0$: $1010010010101010\,0$ and count positions where neighbouring bits differ: 13.
pitfalls: Forgetting the appended $Q_{-1} = 0$ (here it adds nothing because $Q_0 = 0$, but it matters when $Q_0 = 1$).
Counting 1-bits of $Q$ (7) as in ordinary shift-and-add multiplication.
Looking at $M$ — the multiplicand only decides what is added, not how often.
cse-2025-2-cs-22.verification: Transition count in the 17-bit string $1\,0\,1\,0\,0\,1\,0\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0\,0$: the only equal neighbour pairs are $(Q_{12},Q_{11})$, $(Q_9,Q_8)$ and $(Q_0,Q_{-1})$, so $16 - 3 = 13$ changes.

cse-2025-2-cs-23.approach: The loop is Euclid's subtraction algorithm: replacing the larger number by the difference keeps $\gcd(x, y)$ unchanged, and it stops when $x = y$, i.e. at the gcd. So the output is $\gcd(126, 105)$; a short trace confirms it.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: $\gcd(x, y) = \gcd(x - y, y)$, so each iteration preserves the gcd. Values stay positive and strictly decrease, so the loop ends with $x = y = \gcd(126, 105)$.

steps.title: Iterations 4–5, loop exits
steps.body: $y = 63 - 21 = 42$; then $y = 42 - 21 = 21$. Now $x = y = 21$, so `while(x!=y)` is false and the loop ends.

steps.title: Print
steps.body: `printf` prints $x = 21$. Check: $126 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7$, $105 = 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$, $\gcd = 3 \cdot 7 = 21$.

pitfalls: Stopping after the first subtraction (21) for the wrong reason — the loop actually continues until $y$ also reaches 21; the answer is the same only because 21 is the gcd.
Thinking a do-while with equal start values loops forever — here they start unequal.

cse-2025-2-cs-24.approach: Each flip-flop of a ripple counter divides the frequency by 2, so the last of 4 stages runs at $f_{clk}/2^4$. Convert the given period to frequency and multiply by 16.
concepts: Frequency division by 2 per T flip-flop
cse-2025-2-cs-24.given: 4-bit ripple counter; period at the last flip-flop output $= 64\ \mu s$.

steps.title: Each stage divides by 2
steps.body: In a ripple counter every flip-flop is in toggle mode and is clocked by the previous stage's output, so it changes state once per full cycle of its input: its output frequency is half its input frequency. After 4 stages: $f_{Q_3} = f_{clk} / 2^4 = f_{clk}/16$, i.e. $T_{Q_3} = 16\,T_{clk}$.

steps.title: Undo four divide-by-2 stages
steps.body:
$$f_{clk} = 2^4 \times f_{Q_3} = 16 \times 15.625 = 250\ \text{kHz}$$

Equivalently the clock period is $64 / 16 = 4\ \mu s$, and $1 / 4\ \mu s = 250\ \text{kHz}$.

pitfalls: Answering 15.625 kHz (the last stage itself) or dividing instead of multiplying.
Using $2^3$ instead of $2^4$ — each of the 4 flip-flops halves the frequency.
cse-2025-2-cs-24.verification: Going down the chain: 250 → 125 → 62.5 → 31.25 → 15.625 kHz, and $1/15.625\ \text{kHz} = 64\ \mu s$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-25.approach: Insert the keys one by one (each new key walks down from the root, left if smaller, right if larger) and count the comparisons made for 19: the number of nodes it passes equals its depth = number of edges to the root.

steps.title: Insert 10, −4, 15
steps.body: 10 becomes the root; $-4 < 10$ goes left; $15 > 10$ goes right.

steps.title: Insert 19 and count
steps.body:
19: $19 > 10$ → right; $19 > 15$ → right; $19 < 30$ → left; $19 < 20$ → left of 20.

Path to the root: $19 \to 20 \to 30 \to 15 \to 10$, i.e. **4 edges** (19 is at depth 4).

cse-2025-2-cs-25.shortcut: Only keys that 19 is compared with matter: those inserted earlier on its search path — 10, 15, 30, 20. Four ancestors ⇒ 4 edges.
pitfalls: Counting nodes on the path (5) instead of edges (4).
Placing 19 right of 15 directly, forgetting 30 and 20 were inserted before it.
cse-2025-2-cs-25.verification: Ancestors of 19 must be the earlier keys whose range splits around 19: 10 (<19), 15 (<19), 30 (>19), 20 (>19); −4, 5, 60 lie outside its path. 4 ancestors ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-26.approach: In Stop-and-Wait the sender is busy only while transmitting one frame, and each cycle lasts $T_t + 2T_p$ (ACK time negligible). Utilization $U = \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p}$.
cse-2025-2-cs-26.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Frame size $L$ | 3000 bits |
| Rate $B$ | 2000 bps |
| Propagation delay $T_p$ | 100 ms |
| ACK size, processing | negligible |

steps.title: Cycle time
steps.body:
The last bit reaches the receiver at $1.5 + 0.1 = 1.6$ s; the (zero-size) ACK takes another $0.1$ s:

$$T_{cycle} = T_t + 2T_p = 1.5 + 2(0.1) = 1.7\ \text{s}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $93.75\% = 1.5/1.6$ — counts only one propagation delay (forgets the ACK's return trip).
Does not arise from $T_t/(T_t + kT_p)$ with the given data; a distractor.
$66.67\% = 2000/3000$ — divides rate by frame size, mixing up the quantities.

pitfalls: Using $T_t + T_p$ in the denominator (gives 93.75%).
Mixing seconds and milliseconds.
cse-2025-2-cs-26.verification: Frames per second $= 1/1.7$; useful bits per second $= 3000/1.7 \approx 1764.7$; $1764.7/2000 = 88.24\%$ ✓.

cse-2025-2-cs-27.approach: Every spanning tree has exactly $n - 1$ edges, so adding $\alpha$ to every edge shifts **all** spanning-tree weights by the same $(n-1)\alpha$ — the ranking (hence every MST) is unchanged. Paths have different numbers of edges, so path weights shift by different amounts and a shortest path can change; one triangle shows it.

steps.title: MSTs are preserved
steps.body: For any spanning tree $T$: $w'(T) = \sum_{e \in T}(w(e) + \alpha) = w(T) + (n-1)\alpha$. The same constant is added to every spanning tree, so $w(T_1) \le w(T_2) \iff w'(T_1) \le w'(T_2)$. Every MST remains an MST (and no new one appears).

scene.caption: Original weights. MST = {SA, AT} (weight 4). Shortest S→T = S–A–T (4) beats S–T (5).

steps.title: Shortest paths can change
steps.body:
A path with $k$ edges gains $k\alpha$. Take $\alpha = 2$ on the triangle:

| path | edges | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| S–A–T | 2 | $2 + 2 = 4$ | $4 + 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ |
| S–T | 1 | $5$ | $5 + 2 = 7$ |

Before, S–A–T is shortest; after, S–T is. The MST is still {SA, AT} (weight $4 + 2\cdot 2 = 8$ vs. any tree containing ST: $\ge 2 + 5 + 2\cdot2 = 11$).

scene.caption: After adding α = 2: MST still {SA, AT} (8); shortest S→T is now the direct edge (7 < 8).

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.body: MSTs: always preserved. SPs: not necessarily preserved (counterexample above). That is exactly option (C); (A) over-claims, (B) reverses the two, (D) wrongly says MSTs can change.

answer.value: Every MST remains an MST, but SPs need not remain SPs — option **(C)**

optionAnalysis.reason: The triangle example (2, 2, 5 with $\alpha = 2$) changes the shortest S→T path from S–A–T to S–T.
Reversed: MSTs are the ones guaranteed to survive (all spanning trees have $n-1$ edges); SPs are not.
Uniform $(n-1)\alpha$ shift preserves the MST ranking; paths with fewer edges gain less, so SPs may change.
MSTs cannot change — every spanning tree gains exactly $(n-1)\alpha$.

cse-2025-2-cs-27.shortcut: MST: same edge count for every candidate ⇒ invariant. SP: candidates have different edge counts ⇒ not invariant.
pitfalls: Assuming SPs are also preserved because "every edge increased equally".
Confusing this with multiplying weights by a positive constant, which preserves both.
cse-2025-2-cs-27.verification: Kruskal's algorithm only depends on the sorted order of edges, which adding $\alpha$ does not change — so it outputs the same MSTs, confirming the first half independently.

cse-2025-2-cs-28.approach: For each structure pick the cheapest correct meld and argue it is also a lower bound: splice the lists in $O(1)$; concatenate the heap arrays and run linear-time build-heap; flatten both BSTs by in-order traversal, merge the sorted lists and rebuild a BST — all linear.

steps.title: P: doubly linked list — Θ(1)
steps.body: The list is unsorted, so order does not matter. Link $\text{tail}_1 \to \text{head}_2$, $\text{head}_2.\text{prev} = \text{tail}_1$, and set $\text{tail} = \text{tail}_2$: a constant number of pointer updates.

steps.title: Q: array min-heap — Θ(n)
steps.body: Copy both arrays into one array of size $2n$ ($\Theta(n)$), then run bottom-up **build-heap**, which costs $O(2n) = O(n)$ (sum of node heights). Inserting $n$ keys one by one would be $\Theta(n \log n)$ — slower. And copying $n$ elements into one array already needs $\Omega(n)$, so $\Theta(n)$.

steps.title: R: binary search tree — Θ(n)
steps.body: In-order traverse each BST → two sorted lists ($\Theta(n)$); merge them ($\Theta(n)$); build a (balanced) BST from the sorted array by taking the middle as root recursively ($\Theta(n)$). Total $\Theta(n)$. In the worst case the keys of the two trees interleave, so essentially every node must be relinked: $\Omega(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: O(1) splice, concatenate + build-heap in linear time, in-order + merge + rebuild in linear time.
$\Theta(n \log n)$ for the heap assumes inserting the second heap's elements one by one; build-heap does it in $\Theta(n)$.
An unsorted doubly linked list with a tail pointer melds in $O(1)$; $\Theta(n^2)$ for BSTs comes from inserting $n$ keys into a possibly skewed tree — not the best method.
$\Theta(n \log n)$ for BSTs corresponds to inserting keys one by one into a balanced tree; the in-order-merge-rebuild method is linear.

cse-2025-2-cs-28.shortcut: Linked list: pointer splice. Anything that must be rebuilt from $n$ elements in linear time (heap: build-heap, BST: from sorted array) is $\Theta(n)$.
pitfalls: Using repeated insertion as the meld algorithm — the question asks for the best worst-case complexity.
Forgetting that the list is unsorted (a sorted list would need a $\Theta(n)$ merge).
cse-2025-2-cs-28.verification: Lower bounds match: P needs at least one pointer change; Q must place $n$ elements into one array; R must reorganise interleaved keys. Each upper bound meets its lower bound.

cse-2025-2-cs-29.approach: In a direct-mapped cache the physical address splits into tag | index | offset. Block size 1 byte ⇒ 0 offset bits, so the address has $4 + 12 = 16$ bits. Main memory $= 2^{16}$ bytes; cache = (number of lines) × (block size) $= 2^{12} \times 1$ byte.
cse-2025-2-cs-29.given: Tag $= 4$ bits, index $= 12$ bits, block $= 1$ byte (offset $= \log_2 1 = 0$ bits), byte addressable, no extra stored info counted.

steps.title: Address width and main memory
steps.body:
Address bits $= 4 + 12 + 0 = 16$.

$$\text{Main memory} = 2^{16}\ \text{B} = 64 \times 2^{10}\ \text{B} = 64\ \text{KB}$$

steps.title: Cache size
steps.body:
12 index bits ⇒ $2^{12} = 4096$ cache lines, each holding one 1-byte block (tags are not counted — "no other information stored" refers to data capacity):

$$\text{Cache} = 2^{12} \times 1\ \text{B} = 4\ \text{KB}$$

steps.title: Eliminate the other options
steps.body: Any 128 KB main memory needs $\log_2(128 \times 2^{10}) = 17$ address bits, but we have $16$ — kills (B) and (D). (C)'s 8 KB cache would need $2^{13}$ one-byte lines, i.e. 13 index bits. Only (A) fits.

answer.value: **64 KB** main memory and **4 KB** cache — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: 128 KB needs 17 address bits and 16 KB needs 14 index bits — neither matches 4 + 12.
Main memory is right, but 8 KB would need 13 index bits (or 2-byte blocks).
6 KB $= 4096 \times (8 + 4)$ bits counts the tag storage too, which the question excludes; and 128 KB would need a 17-bit address.

pitfalls: Adding tag bits into the cache size (4096 × (8 + 4) bits = 6 KB, option D's trap).
Assuming some offset bits even though the block is 1 byte.
cse-2025-2-cs-29.verification: Ratio main/cache $= 64/4 = 16 = 2^4$ — exactly the number of memory blocks competing for each line, which is what 4 tag bits distinguish ✓.
